blocks.text: Every resource needs a name that never changes meaning, something a client can hold onto, pass around, log, and use months later to fetch the exact same thing again. That name is the resource's URI.
It looks a lot like a web address, and in some cases it literally is one, but MCP stretches the idea further, letting a server invent its own scheme for whatever it is exposing.
This lesson is entirely about that string: what it is made of, how it is structured, and the conventions that keep it useful across very different kinds of servers.
1. Why Resources Need a URI at All

A resource without a stable identifier would be nearly useless beyond the single moment it was fetched. The whole point of exposing something as a resource is that a client can refer back to it, cache it, ask for it again to see if it changed, or pass its identifier along to another part of a system. The URI is what makes all of that possible, it is the one piece of information that always uniquely names a specific resource within a given server.

This is exactly the same job a URL does on the web, and MCP deliberately borrows that idea rather than inventing something new. If you have ever bookmarked a page, shared a link, or noticed that changing one character in a URL takes you somewhere completely different, you already understand the core behavior a resource URI needs to have.

Without a durable identifier, a host application would have no way to say "fetch that same log file again" a few turns later in a conversation, it would have to re-run discovery from scratch every single time. The URI is what turns a resource from a one-off answer into something genuinely referenceable, which is exactly the property a long running assistant needs.
2. The Anatomy of a URI

blocks.alt: A URI is built from a scheme, an authority, and a path
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738931-944866960.png

A URI is built from a small number of parts, not all of which every scheme uses. The scheme comes first, followed by a colon, telling the client what kind of resource this is and how the rest of the string should be parsed. After that typically comes an authority, often introduced by two slashes, naming a host or a namespace, and finally a path, identifying the specific thing within that namespace.

code.content:
file:///Users/dev/project/README.md
\_/  \______________________________/
scheme          path

postgres://orders-db/customers/48213
\______/  \______/ \________________/
 scheme   authority       path

blocks.text: Not every part is mandatory for every scheme. What matters is that within a single scheme, the structure stays consistent, so a client that has seen one URI from a server can reasonably guess the shape of another.

It helps to compare this to something you already parse every day without thinking about it, an email address. The part after the @ tells you which mail server to route through, the part before it identifies a specific mailbox on that server. A resource URI's scheme and authority and path play very similar, complementary roles.
3. The Scheme: What Kind of Resource This Is

blocks.alt: Different schemes mark different kinds of resources
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738932-770811494.png

The scheme is the part before the first colon, and it is the single most important piece of a resource URI, because it tells a client what universe of rules to apply to everything that follows. file means a location in a file system. https means an ordinary web resource. A custom scheme like ticket or postgres means the server has defined its own private convention that only makes sense in the context of that particular server.

blocks.text: A client that recognizes a scheme can sometimes offer richer handling, rendering a file:// resource with syntax highlighting based on its extension, or an https:// resource as a live link, while falling back to plain text display for a scheme it does not specifically recognize. Recognizing a scheme is always optional, never required, for correct behavior.
4. Standard Schemes vs Custom Schemes

When a resource genuinely corresponds to something the internet already has a URI format for, a file, a web page, use that existing scheme rather than reinventing one. This is what lets a generic client render a file:// resource sensibly without needing server specific knowledge. But plenty of resources have no natural existing URI format, a row in a database, an entry in a proprietary system, and for those, servers are free to invent their own scheme.

None of these custom schemes are registered with any official body, and that is fine. MCP does not require a scheme to be globally recognized, only that it is used consistently within the server that defines it, and ideally documented clearly enough that a client author knows how to interpret it.
A custom scheme is perfectly valid as long as it is documented and used consistently by the server that defines it, a client does not need to recognize a scheme in advance to work with it correctly.
5. The Authority: Naming a Namespace

blocks.alt: The authority names a namespace that a path sits inside
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439739262-633286189.png

When a scheme has an authority component, it usually names a host, a database, or some other namespace the path is relative to. In postgres://orders-db/customers/48213, orders-db is the authority, telling you which database this identifier belongs to, separate from the path customers/48213 that identifies the specific row within it.

Not every scheme needs an authority. file:// URIs typically use an empty authority, which is why you see three slashes in a row, file, colon, two slashes for an empty authority, then one more slash to start the absolute path.

When a server only ever exposes one namespace, a single database, a single file system root, the authority segment sometimes gets left empty or set to a fixed placeholder, since there is nothing to distinguish between. It only earns its keep once a server genuinely spans multiple distinct namespaces a client needs to tell apart.
Two servers using the same authority string does not imply any relationship between them, authority is only meaningful within the context of the specific server that assigned it.
6. The Path: Identifying the Specific Thing

The path is usually where the real specificity lives, the part that narrows a URI down from an entire namespace to one exact resource. For files, this is a familiar file system path. For a custom scheme, the path might be a numeric identifier, a slug, a hierarchical category, whatever structure makes the most sense for the underlying data.
7. Query Parameters and Fragments

Just like ordinary web URLs, a resource URI can include a query string after a question mark, or a fragment after a hash sign, when that makes sense for the scheme. A server might use a query parameter to express a filter or a version, for instance.

These are useful, but they add complexity, and a server author should only reach for them when a simpler path segment would not do the job just as clearly. A URI that is easy to read at a glance is worth far more than one that is technically expressive but opaque.

One good rule of thumb, if you find yourself wanting to add more than one or two query parameters to express what a resource is, that is often a sign the underlying concept should be split into several distinct resources with their own clear paths instead, rather than one resource with many optional variations bolted onto its URI.
Not every resource needs query parameters or a fragment, a simple resource can be identified by scheme, authority, and path alone, these extra pieces exist for the cases that genuinely need them.
8. URIs Must Be Stable

blocks.alt: A stable URI is compared against one that changes between calls
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439739264-792090974.png

The single most important property of a good resource URI is stability: the same URI should keep meaning the same underlying resource over time, even as that resource's content changes. A file's content can be edited every day, but file:///project/README.md should still refer to the README, not to a different file entirely. Stability is what makes caching, re-reading, and referencing across a conversation actually work.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Content can change, identity should not. If a URI needs to point at a genuinely different thing, mint a new URI rather than repurposing an old one.

blocks.text: 8.1 What Happens When Something Is Deleted

If the underlying thing a URI pointed to genuinely stops existing, a file gets deleted, a database row gets removed, the URI should not silently start pointing at something else. A resources/read call against a URI whose target no longer exists should return a clear error, not quietly resolve to a different, unrelated resource that happens to reuse the same identifier.
9. URIs Are Opaque to the Client

blocks.alt: A client treats a URI as an opaque string rather than parsing it
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439739264-210771485.png

A client should treat a resource URI as an opaque string to be passed back to the server, not something to parse and reinterpret on its own, beyond reading the scheme to decide broadly how to handle it. The client does not need to understand that postgres://orders-db/customers/48213 implies a specific SQL query, it just needs to hand that string back to resources/read and trust the server to resolve it correctly.

This opacity is a feature, not a limitation. It means a server is free to change its internal implementation, switch databases, restructure storage, without breaking any client, as long as the URIs it already handed out keep resolving to the same content.
A client should never try to parse meaning out of a path beyond what the server has documented, treating the whole URI as an opaque identifier is the safest default.
9.1 A Quick Analogy

Think of a URI the way you think of a phone number. You do not need to understand a phone company's internal routing to dial a number and reach the right person, you just need the number itself to stay correctly assigned to that person over time. A resource URI works the same way, the server handles all the routing behind the scenes.
10. How a Client Encounters URIs

In practice, a client rarely invents resource URIs from scratch. Almost always it receives them from a resources/list call, and simply holds onto them to use later in a resources/read call. The exception is resource templates, covered two lessons from now, where a client does construct a URI itself by filling in a parameterized pattern the server advertised.

This is also why servers should avoid surprising a client with a URI shape it has never seen documented anywhere, resources/list is the primary way a client learns the vocabulary of what a server's URIs look like, and a server that hands back wildly inconsistent shapes makes that discovery process far less useful.

blocks.title: Where URIs show up
blocks.content: A client typically first sees a resource URI in the response to resources/list, then uses that exact same URI later when calling resources/read.

blocks.text: 11. Naming Conventions Worth Following

items: Keep the scheme lowercase and descriptive, ticket rather than Ticket or T.
Use forward slashes to express hierarchy, the same way file paths and web paths already do, since it reads naturally.
Avoid embedding secrets, tokens, or credentials directly in a URI, since URIs tend to get logged and displayed.
Prefer stable identifiers, such as a database primary key or a slug, over anything that might shift, such as a row's position in a result set.
Keep URIs human-scannable where possible, a person glancing at a resource list should be able to guess roughly what each URI points to.

blocks.text: Consistency matters more than any single rule on this list. A server that picks a convention, hierarchical paths, lowercase schemes, no trailing slashes, and applies it uniformly across every resource it exposes will always be easier for a client to work with than one that technically follows every best practice but applies them inconsistently from one resource to the next.
12. Case Sensitivity and Encoding

blocks.alt: Case sensitivity and encoding rules affect whether two URIs match
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439739265-356393414.png

Scheme names are conventionally lowercase, and most implementations treat them case sensitively, so pick one casing and stick to it consistently across an entire server. Special characters inside a path, spaces, unicode characters, punctuation, should be percent-encoded the same way a web URL would encode them, so that a URI remains a single unambiguous token rather than something that might be misparsed by different tools.
When in doubt, treat a URI as case sensitive and avoid manually re-encoding characters a server already returned, mismatched encoding is a common source of silent lookup failures.
13. Comparing URIs Across Servers

When a client is connected to multiple MCP servers at once, a common and important habit is scoping resources by which server they came from before doing anything with the raw URI, since two entirely unrelated servers could both define a scheme called config:// that means something completely different in each case. The URI alone is only meaningful in the context of the specific server that issued it.

Two different servers can use the exact same scheme for entirely unrelated things, a client should never assume a scheme means the same thing across two servers it has not explicitly confirmed are related.
14. Reserved and Common Schemes to Know

blocks.content: {"headers":["Scheme","Typical use in MCP servers"],"rows":[["file","Local or mounted file system paths"],["https","Publicly reachable web resources"],["git","A specific commit, branch, or file within a repository"],["s3","An object inside a cloud storage bucket"],["custom scheme","Anything specific to the server's own domain"]]}

blocks.text: When in doubt about whether to use an existing scheme or invent a new one, check whether a client is likely to already have special handling for that scheme built in. Reusing file:// gets you free syntax highlighting and familiar rendering in many host applications, inventing myapp-file:// gets you none of that for no real benefit.
15. When to Invent a New Scheme

blocks.alt: No existing scheme fitting points toward inventing a new one
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439739265-404950742.png

Reach for a brand new custom scheme only when nothing standard fits, and when doing so, name it after the domain concept it represents rather than after your company or project. crm:// reads clearly to any future maintainer, acmecorp-internal-system-7:// does not. A well chosen scheme name is documentation in itself.

A new scheme is worth inventing when the resource genuinely does not fit an existing convention, reusing an established scheme like file or http, even loosely, is usually clearer than inventing one unnecessarily.
Worked Example
Consider a server exposing a company wiki. A sensible scheme might be wiki://, with the authority naming the specific wiki space and the path naming the article by its slug.

A client browsing this server's resources/list would see these three URIs alongside human readable names, and could immediately tell, just from the authority segment, which team's wiki each article belongs to, without needing to fetch a single one of them first.
Common Mistakes

items: Reusing the same URI for two genuinely different pieces of content instead of minting a new one when the underlying thing changes.
Parsing a resource URI's internal structure on the client side and hardcoding assumptions about a specific server's scheme.
Embedding an API key, password, or session token directly inside a URI string.
Mixing casing inconsistently across a server's own custom scheme, making URIs harder to compare or search.
Choosing an identifier that can shift over time, like a row's position in a result set, instead of a stable key.
Treating a URI from one server as meaningful when handed to a different, unrelated server.

blocks.text: Practice

Design a URI scheme for an MCP server that exposes calendar events. Decide on a scheme name, whether it needs an authority, and what the path should encode. Write out three example URIs for different events.
Key Takeaway

A resource URI is the stable name every resource needs, built from a scheme that says how to interpret the rest of the string, and usually an authority and a path that narrow things down to one specific thing. Standard schemes should be reused when they genuinely fit, custom schemes are fine and common when they do not, and above all, a URI should stay opaque to the client and stable over time.

The next lesson looks at static resources, the simplest category of resource a server can expose, a fixed and known set that does not change from one moment to the next, and how a server declares that fixed set up front.
